ao_demand_evidence.input: Suggest why one root-tip field with few visibly dividing cells cannot show that mitosis has stopped throughout the root.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The field samples only a few cells at a single moment. Other fields, or other moments, may contain more dividing cells, so several fields should be examined.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Fig. VIS-6116-4.1-07 is a photomicrograph of cells from a prepared slide of reproductive tissue showing meiosis. Draw a large labelled biological drawing of the cells in one part of the field.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: A large drawing of the cells in one chosen area, in clear continuous unshaded lines and in the proportions seen. The cell outlines and the visible nuclear material or chromosomes are drawn accurately. Labels are ruled lines that touch the structures and do not cross, and the drawing has a title and a magnification.

ao_demand_evidence.input: An animal cell has two pairs of chromosomes: M1 and P1 form one pair, and M2 and P2 form the other (M is from the mother and P from the father). Meiosis produces a gamete containing M1 and P2. Explain what this shows about how meiosis shares out maternal and paternal chromosomes.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The gamete contains one chromosome from each pair, but M1 is maternal and P2 is paternal. So meiosis does not put all the maternal chromosomes in one gamete and all the paternal ones in another; it makes mixed combinations.

ao_demand_evidence.input: A grower clones one high-yield plant, but a new disease kills that genotype. Suggest why planting the whole field with clones of this plant is risky despite the yield advantage.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The clones all have the same susceptible genotype, so the new disease can spread through the whole field. The high yield is lost if all the plants die.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Two crop populations grow equally well now. One is a single clone; the other contains plants with different alleles, one of which tolerates a forecast rise in soil salt. Suggest which population is more likely to survive that change.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The varied population is more likely to survive, because it already contains salt-tolerant plants that can survive and reproduce. The clone has no such plants.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Fig. VIS-6116-4.2.2-05 is a photograph of an insect-pollinated flower viewed through a hand lens, showing its anthers and stigma. Draw and label the anther and the stigma.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: A large drawing in clear single unshaded lines, with the anther and the stigma in correct proportion and position. The anther and stigma are labelled with ruled lines that touch the parts, and the drawing has a title and magnification.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Fig. VIS-6116-4.2.2-06 shows an insect-pollinated flower and a wind-pollinated flower side by side. Draw each flower’s anthers and stigmas and label them.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: Two large clear drawings with proportionate parts. The wind-pollinated flower has anthers and stigmas outside the flower, the stigma being large and feathery. The insect-pollinated flower has them within or among the petals. Anthers and stigmas are labelled, and each drawing has a title naming the type of flower.

ao_demand_evidence.input: A flowering plant grows alone, far from other plants of its species, and no pollinating insects visit it. It is able to self-pollinate. Suggest why it can still produce seeds, and give one genetic disadvantage of this.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: Its pollen can reach a stigma on the same plant, so fertilisation can happen without another plant. The offspring have alleles from one plant only, so there is less variation.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Pollen forms very few tubes in a very concentrated sugar solution. Suggest why this does not show that pollen cannot use sugar for respiration.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: A very concentrated solution can draw water out of the pollen grains by osmosis, which stops them growing. So the failure may be caused by water loss, not by an inability to use sugar.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Many seeds fall densely beneath a parent plant in deep shade; a few reach equally moist open soil. Explain why the seedlings in open soil may establish better even though they are farther from the parent.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: They receive more light and have less competition from the parent and from other seedlings. The soil is equally moist, so the greater distance does not cause a water shortage.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Explain why a treatment that strongly suppresses FSH can prevent normal egg release even though the oviduct is not blocked.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: Without FSH the follicles do not develop properly, so no mature egg is ready for release. An open oviduct does not help if there is no mature egg.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Explain why a mature follicle may not release its egg if the LH surge does not happen.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The follicle can be mature, but ovulation is triggered by the LH surge. Without it the egg is not released and no corpus luteum forms.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Explain why a woman whose oestrogen stays low throughout the first half of the cycle may have both a thin uterus lining and no LH surge.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: Oestrogen is needed to build the lining, so a low level leaves it thin. A high level of oestrogen is needed to stimulate the LH surge, so the surge does not occur.

ao_demand_evidence.input: A woman’s cycle has normal ovulation, but her progesterone level falls earlier than usual. Explain why her uterus lining may be shed early.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The lining depends on progesterone to be maintained. When the level falls early, the support is lost early, so the lining breaks down early. Normal ovulation does not prevent this.

ao_demand_evidence.input: A study finds fewer infections among breastfed babies, but the groups differ in water sanitation and household crowding. Suggest why the figures alone cannot measure the protective effect of the antibodies in milk.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: Sanitation and crowding also affect how often babies are exposed to infection, and they differ between the groups. So the difference may be due to them and not to the antibodies.

ao_demand_evidence.input: A clinic gives out contraceptive pills free of charge, but few couples in the community use them because cultural and religious beliefs discourage contraception. Suggest why free supply alone does not mean that contraception will be used, and one way the clinic could respond respectfully.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: People’s decisions depend on their beliefs and information as well as cost, so free pills may still be unused. The clinic could offer clear, respectful information and counselling so that people can make their own informed choices.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Two groups have similar exposure to the bacteria that cause TB, but the group with untreated advanced HIV has more severe cases. Suggest a biological explanation without assuming that they were more exposed.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: Their immune systems are weakened by HIV, so they cannot control the bacteria as well. Because their exposure is the same, the difference is in their defences.

ao_demand_evidence.input: A household loses some paid work time because of illness, but it then receives effective treatment and transport to the clinic. Suggest why a forecast that assumes the household will lose its income permanently may overestimate the effect.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: With treatment the person can recover health and return to work, and transport support lowers the cost of care. The forecast ignores these given measures.

ao_demand_evidence.input: No seeds germinate in the test condition or in the favourable comparison. Suggest why this prevents a clear conclusion about the test condition.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The seeds may be dead, or the method may be faulty. If the favourable comparison fails, the failure in the test condition cannot be put down to the condition.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Calculate the percentage germination when 21 of 30 seeds germinate.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: 21 ÷ 30 = 0.7; 0.7 × 100 = 70, so the percentage germination is 70%.

ao_demand_evidence.input: A sample of fresh seeds has 21 of 30 germinating, and a sample of seeds stored for a year has 24 of 40 germinating. Show your working, then complete the sentence: the fresh seeds give __% germination and the stored seeds __%, so the higher percentage is for the __ seeds.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The fresh seeds have the higher percentage, at 70%, compared with 60% for the stored seeds.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Two stored seed batches have 90% and 55% germination, but they are different varieties tested at different temperatures. Suggest why storage time alone cannot explain the difference.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: Variety and test temperature can also change germination. Because both differ between the batches, the difference cannot be put down to storage time alone.

ao_demand_evidence.input: A plant grown in shade is taller than an equally old plant grown in good light, but it has less dry mass. Suggest why height alone would misrepresent their growth.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The shaded plant has stretched upwards without making as much material. Its lower dry mass shows that it has grown less, so the height is misleading.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Two genes contain the same numbers of A, T, C and G bases, but in different orders, and they code for different amino acid sequences. Explain why equal base totals do not mean that the proteins are the same.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The code depends on the order of the bases, not on their totals. The different amino acid sequences given will fold into different proteins with different functions.

ao_demand_evidence.input: A cell receives a normal amount of a neurotransmitter, but it makes receptors with an altered binding region. Explain why its response may be reduced.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The altered receptor may bind the neurotransmitter poorly. The signal is therefore received less well, even though the amount of neurotransmitter is normal.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Approved heterozygous cross and small sample.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: Derive the one-quarter outcome and qualify realised counts by sampling chance.

ao_demand_evidence.input: An unknown purple-flowered plant is crossed with a white-flowered plant (aa), where A is dominant to a. The offspring are five purple and four white. Deduce the genotype of the purple parent and explain.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The purple parent is Aa. The white offspring (aa) must each have received an a from both parents, and the purple parent is purple because it has A. The offspring are close to 1:1, as expected for Aa × aa.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Draw a genetic diagram for cattle coat colour, in which CᴿCᴿ is red, CᵂCᵂ is white and CᴿCᵂ is roan. A roan animal is crossed with a white animal. Give the phenotype ratio of the offspring.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: Parental phenotypes: roan × white. Genotypes: CᴿCᵂ × CᵂCᵂ. Gametes: Cᴿ or Cᵂ; Cᵂ. Offspring: CᴿCᵂ and CᵂCᵂ, equally likely. Ratio: 1 roan : 1 white.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Draw a genetic diagram for an X-linked recessive condition, in which Xᴺ is the unaffected allele, Xⁿ is the allele for the condition and Y has no matching allele. Cross an unaffected carrier female XᴺXⁿ with an unaffected male XᴺY and give the proportion of all offspring that are affected.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: Parents: unaffected carrier female × unaffected male, XᴺXⁿ × XᴺY. Gametes: Xᴺ or Xⁿ; Xᴺ or Y. Offspring: XᴺXᴺ unaffected female, XᴺXⁿ carrier female, XᴺY unaffected male, XⁿY affected male. Proportion affected: 1/4, or 25%.

ao_demand_evidence.input: A learner removes the counters that have been drawn from small R and r bags instead of replacing them. Suggest why this stops the simulation from representing independent fertilisations.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: Removing the counters changes the proportions of R and r left in each bag, so the chance of each gamete changes from one draw to the next. Replacing them keeps the chances the same for each offspring.

ao_demand_evidence.input: The lengths of eight leaves are 31, 34, 38, 42, 45, 47, 51 and 54 mm. Give the number of leaves in each class: 30–39, 40–49 and 50–59 mm. State which class or classes have the highest frequency.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The counts are 3, 3 and 2. The classes 30–39 mm and 40–49 mm are tied for the highest frequency.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Two populations start with the same frequency of the sickle-cell allele. Severe malaria is common in one but absent from the other. Explain why the allele may remain common in the malaria population but become rarer in the other.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: Where malaria occurs, heterozygotes survive better, so the allele stays. Where there is no malaria, the allele only causes disease in homozygotes, so it is selected against.
